sub_scenario.one_line: rail service recovery chief: prepare the sequence board for the deputy and lead tomorrow's recovery review

dialogue.content: I spent the first hour tidying the traction sequence board and closing stale entries.
Anything still open?
Two items, both with owners.
The disruption rota review wrapped early today.
Any surprises in it?
None worth recording.
I lead planned daytime service changes well with the traction sequence board in front of me.
Why does that help?
It makes power isolation, train positioning, and crew release visible in one order.
Someone new shadowed me in the control room this morning.
Did that slow you down?
A little, but the questions were good ones.
I batched my replies about the night incidents into one message before lunch.
Cleaner than drip-feeding answers.
Much cleaner.
When a substation fault stopped the east line, I mapped power clearance before moving replacement buses and reopened safely.
What did the map prevent?
It stopped us sending buses before the stranded trains could be released.
I can take a short late-afternoon depot update after ordinary work.
Does that prove a night emergency is suitable?
No. A depot update does not commit passenger recovery under pressure.
I archived last cycle's notes on the disruption rota and set up the new folder.
A fresh start?
As fresh as these things get.
I finished an all-night weather disruption at dawn and have a mandated recovery day after it.
Can you waive the day?
No. It exists because fatigue has affected command decisions before.
A vendor call about the traction sequence board ran long but ended well.
Worth the time?
This one, yes.
I walked through the control room checklist with the new starter.
How did they do?
Careful and quick, a good sign.
Quiet afternoon; I cleared the backlog around the night incidents.
A rare day.
I did not waste it.
I flagged a small inconsistency in the disruption rota records and fixed it at the source.
Root cause or symptom?
Root cause, for once.
During a snow-night incident without the sequence board, I dispatched buses before confirming platform clearance and created a second bottleneck.
What was missing?
The dependency order and the rest to reason through it.
I sketched next week's plan for the night incidents before leaving.
Ahead of schedule?
Ahead enough to sleep well.
Lunch walk, then a clean pass through the traction sequence board updates.
Does the walk help?
It resets the afternoon.
My sleep specialist has asked me to keep the recovery day after night duty; a rested deputy can cover tonight's room.
Is there another workable route?
Yes, I can prepare the board for the deputy and return tomorrow.
I compared two options for the disruption rota tooling and noted a mild preference.
Decision made?
Deferred until the trial ends.
I closed the week by updating the control room handover notes.
Anything unusual to hand over?
Blessedly little.
The director asks me to chair a 00:30 rail-recovery war room after last night's weather disruption. How should I respond?
